cards.summary: A beat sheet a creator films on a phone so a paid ad looks and sounds like a real customer talking: several hook options, a relatable problem, the product working on camera, one proof moment and a call to action in the creator's own words, with the ad disclosure built in. YouTube Shorts and in-feed ads that need a native, unpolished look
Briefing creators hired through UGC marketplaces or agencies (one beat sheet, several creators)

Marketplace and app-install video where a face and a hand-held demo outperform a brand film

cards.goal: The viewer stops scrolling, believes a real person uses the product, and taps the ad's button (Shop now, Install, Learn more).

structure.does: Product, the single message, who the viewer is, format (9:16, sound on with captions), length, tone, must-say lines (exact), must-not-say list (claims the brand cannot prove, competitor names), disclosure label and where it appears, deliverables (e.g. 4 hooks x 1 body).

3-5 alternative openings, each a spoken line plus the visual action (product in hand, reaction, mid-task, on-screen text). Each must work muted through the text overlay. Start mid-action, never with a greeting or a logo.
structure.length: 0-3 seconds each; one line under about 12 words

structure.does: The specific annoyance in the words a customer uses (mine reviews and comments), shown rather than described: the sweaty forehead, the tangled cable, the burnt tawa.
The product used on camera with one visible result and one concrete detail (texture, time taken, the click of the lid). Mark which lines are 'say it your way' and which claim is 'say exactly'.
Answer the one doubt that stops purchase (price, skin type, size, 'does it really work') or show real reviews the brand can produce on request.
One action in the creator's own words that matches the ad button, the offer if any (code, price), an on-screen CTA line, and the disclosure label superimposed for the time ASCI requires.
B-roll list (unboxing, close-ups, before/after only if real and unexaggerated) and the on-screen text lines in order, so the editor can cut variants.

length.note: Whole beat sheet: brief header, hook options, beats and shot list. The spoken body is short (15-45 seconds is the usual ask); time it by reading aloud at the creator's pace, since Hindi and Hinglish pace varies by speaker. More hook variants and more creators push the brief up, not the spoken length.

checklist: Are there at least 3 distinct hook options, each one spoken line with its visual action?
Does every hook start mid-action, with no greeting, intro or logo first?
Is the product on screen or in hand within the first few seconds of every hook?
Is the problem stated in a customer's words, not in brand claims?
Is there a demo beat where the product is used on camera with one visible result?
Are must-say claims listed separately, and could the brand prove each one if asked?
Is the disclosure label (Ad, Sponsored, Collaboration, Partnership or Paid Partnership) named with when and where it appears on screen?
Does the CTA ask for one action that matches the ad's button?
Are there on-screen text lines so the ad works with sound off?
Are health, finance or result claims limited to the creator's honest experience, with no promised outcomes?
pitfalls: A brand script the creator reads word for word: it sounds like an ad and gets skipped. Write beats and one or two exact must-say lines; let the creator paraphrase the rest.
One hook only: UGC ads are bought by testing openings. Give 3-5 hooks over the same body so the media buyer can find the winner.

Scripting fake history ('I've used this for six months') for a creator who got the product last week: ASCI needs disclosure of any material connection, including free product, and the claim itself misleads. Script 'I've been trying this for [actual period]'.

Health or money results ('cleared my acne in 7 days', 'saved me Rs 20,000'): ASCI's Addendum II asks for qualifications for health and finance talk. Keep to experience language and claims the brand already substantiates.
Disclosure only in the caption or at the end: ASCI wants it upfront and superimposed; a 15-second video needs the label for at least 3 seconds, a 15 s to 2 min video for a third of its length.
Before/after shots that exaggerate: real, same lighting, same angle, or none at all.
Hinglish written in stiff textbook Hindi: write how the creator talks ('yaar, ye stick bag mein rehti hai'), then let them change words.
cards.exemplar_brief: UGC ad beat sheet for a Pune D2C brand's Rs 499 sunscreen stick aimed at two-wheeler commuters; creator: a 24-year-old college student in Pune; Hinglish (Roman script); 30-second 9:16 Instagram Reels partnership ad; 4 hook options, problem-demo-proof-CTA beats, on-screen text lines, must-say claim 'SPF 50, no white cast' and ASCI disclosure placement; goal: tap Shop Now.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. All seven parts in order: brief header with exact must-say ('SPF 50, no white cast') and a sharp must-not-say list (tan nahi hoga, waterproof, dermat-approved, 'X din' results); 4 hooks, each a spoken line + visual + muted text, all mid-action with the stick in hand; problem in customer words ('chehra safed, helmet ke neeche chipchip'); demo with same-angle/same-light check; price objection; CTA matches Shop Now. ASCI placement is right: 'Ad' + Paid partnership on screen from 0:00 for at least 10 s (a third of 30 s), caption starts 'Ad', free-product disclosure. Natural Roman Hinglish. Nit: 518 words vs the card's 450 max. CARD FIX (minor): length.max 450 -> 600 to match lint.max_words, since a 4-hook sheet with every structure part lands near 500. | CARD FIXED 2026-10-07 (fix_genre_d): length.max 450 -> 600 to match lint.max_words; re-judge pending.

cards.name: Ultimate guide / long-form article
cards.summary: The one page that covers a topic end to end so a searcher never needs a second tab: clear scope, key takeaways up top, a table of contents with jump links, and sections that each answer one sub-question first and then go deep. Good looks like first-hand examples, tables and steps a skimmer can find in seconds, and a last-updated date, not a word count padded to beat a competitor.
use_for: Broad-intent search topics ('home loan guide for first-time buyers') where readers need the whole picture
The reference page a brand links to from sales emails, onboarding and support
Link-earning resources that other sites cite
Pages meant to be quoted by AI search answers (clear, answer-first sections)
avoid: A single narrow question ('how to link PAN with Aadhaar'): use genre:how_to_article or genre:faq_answer_article
A hub that mostly summarises and links out to cluster pages: use genre:pillar_page
A gated download traded for an email: use genre:ebook_lead_magnet
Padding to match the longest competitor: Google's spam policies target scaled, low-value content; cover the questions, then stop
Rewriting the top results with nothing new: add first-hand steps, screenshots, local specifics or data the others lack

cards.goal: The searcher gets every answer they came for without returning to the results page, then takes the page's one next step (tool, sign-up, product) or bookmarks it.

structure.does: Keyword first, scope stated (who it is for, year if facts change), promise of completeness without hype.
Who the guide is for, what they will be able to do after it, why trust the writer (first-hand experience, credentials), last-updated date.
The direct answer to the main question in bullets, so a hurried reader or an AI summary gets it right.
One jump link per H2, worded as the question or task the section answers.

Ordered along the reader's journey (basics, decision, setup, advanced). Each opens with a 40-60-word direct answer, then steps, examples, tables, screenshots notes and local specifics. End each with a one-line bridge to the next.
One real end-to-end case: a named situation, the numbers, what was done, the result. This is where the page earns citations.
5-8 questions people actually ask (support tickets, People Also Ask, comments), each answered in 2-4 sentences.
One CTA that fits the reader's stage, plus 3-5 descriptive internal links to deeper pages.

length.note: Set by the number of sub-questions the searcher has, not by competitor word counts. A focused consumer topic is often 2,000-3,000 words; a B2B or regulatory topic with many branches can reach 6,000+. If a section grows past about 800 words, it probably deserves its own page linked from here.

checklist: Does the intro say who the guide is for and what they will be able to do after reading?
Is there a key-takeaways block near the top that answers the main question?
Is there a table of contents whose entries match the H2s?
Does every H2 section open with a direct answer before the detail?
Is there at least one worked example with real numbers or a real case?
Is every statistic, rule or price either sourced or removed?
Are there India-specific details (rupee amounts, Indian forms, local examples) where the audience is Indian?
Is there a last-updated date?
Does the page end with one clear next step and descriptive internal links (no 'click here')?
Could any section be deleted without the reader missing it? (If yes, delete it.)
pitfalls: A 600-word intro on 'why this topic matters': the reader already searched for it. Give the answer in the key takeaways and start section one by line 10.
Sections titled by the writer's labels ('Overview', 'Considerations'): title them with the reader's question ('How much sunlight does a balcony need?').
Repeating the same point in every section to hit a length: cut it and add a table, checklist or example instead.
Facts with no date in a fast-moving topic (tax limits, app features): date them, link the official source, and schedule a refresh (genre:content_refresh).
One giant wall of text: use steps, tables and short paragraphs; most readers jump straight to one section from the table of contents.
Generic stock advice any AI could produce: add the first-hand detail (what went wrong, the exact setting that worked, a photo note).

ban.label: filler intro phrases
ban.regex: (?i)without further ado|in this (comprehensive|ultimate) guide,? we will

cards.exemplar_brief: Ultimate guide for a Pune seed-and-planter D2C brand: 'Balcony vegetable gardening in Indian cities: the complete guide'; audience: first-time apartment gardeners in Pune, Bengaluru and Hyderabad; English; 2,000-2,500 words with key takeaways, table of contents, sections on sunlight, containers, soil mix, what to grow by season, watering and pests, one worked example of a 4-pot starter balcony, FAQs; no invented statistics; goal: shop the starter kit.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. Title tag 57 chars and meta 147; intro says who it is for and what they can do, with a last-updated date and a marked trust placeholder; key takeaways answer the question; TOC matches the H2s, each H2 is the reader's question and opens with a 40-60-word direct answer; tables for containers, seasons and pests; city-specific notes for Pune, Bengaluru and Hyderabad; 4-pot worked example labelled illustrative (no real case supplied) with soil volume that reconciles (20+12+~25+8 = 65 L); timings hedged, no invented stats; one CTA to the starter kit plus 5 descriptive internal links. Nits: the end-of-section bridges are formulaic ('Plans meet questions...'); FAQs at 5 are the card's floor and do not cover mistakes as the H2 promises.

cards.name: Upsell / one-time-offer (OTO) page
cards.summary: The page shown right after payment that offers one add-on which makes the purchase work better or faster, with a single yes button and an equally plain 'no thanks'. Good looks like: order confirmed first, a short reason the add-on fits what they just bought, an honest price, one click to accept, and a polite decline that never shames.
use_for: Course and ebook funnels (template pack, coaching call, community access after the main product)
D2C post-purchase offers (refill pack, matching accessory, subscription switch)
SaaS upgrades shown after a monthly purchase (annual plan, add-on seats)
Downsell pages shown after an upsell is declined
Order-bump checkbox lines on the checkout page
avoid: An unrelated product: the offer must extend what was just bought, or it reads as a bait
The full sales argument for a new, expensive product: use genre:sales_page or genre:vsl_script
Checkout fields and payment reassurance: use genre:order_form_checkout_copy
Building the offer itself (bonuses, guarantee, value stack): use genre:offer_stack
Guilt lines on the decline link ('No, I'd rather stay broke'): CCPA's dark-pattern guidelines name confirm shaming; write a neutral 'No thanks, continue to my order'
Fake countdowns or 'only on this page' claims that are not true: false urgency is also a listed dark pattern

buyers: Course creators and coaches selling through funnels

cards.value_why: Rarely bought alone: it comes inside sales-funnel packages (Upwork's sales funnel copywriting category, 2026-10-04), so it is priced as a page within a bundle.
cards.goal: The buyer clicks yes to the add-on (or the cheaper downsell) without doubting the order they just placed, or declines in one click and still feels good about the brand.

structure.does: Says the order went through and what happens next, so the buyer is not anxious. Optionally, 'one more thing before you go'.
Connects the add-on to what they just bought and the result it speeds up.
Names what the main purchase leaves slow or unsolved, in the buyer's terms, without criticising the main product.
What it is, what they get, and 3-5 outcome bullets. If there is a video, this text summarises it.
The one-time price, an honest comparison only if that regular price is genuinely charged elsewhere, and why it is cheaper here (no extra checkout, bundle saving).
First-person label naming the item and price: 'Yes, add the template pack for Rs 499'. Note one-click charging if the card is saved.
Neutral, same visibility as a normal link: 'No thanks, take me to my order'.
A smaller or cheaper version with one line on what is different.

length.note: Short because the buyer is mid-flow. A low-price add-on needs 100-200 words; a higher-priced coaching or annual-plan upsell may need 300-400 words or a short video (write that as a mini genre:vsl_script).

checklist: Does the page confirm the original order before pitching anything?
Is the add-on clearly connected to what was just bought?
Is the price stated in full, with no hidden charges added later?
Is any 'regular price' comparison one the seller genuinely charges?
Does the yes button name the item and the price?
Is there a plain decline link with no guilt or fear wording?
Is any deadline or 'only here' claim literally true?
Can the page be read in under a minute?
pitfalls: Opening with the pitch while the buyer is still unsure the payment worked: confirm the order first, then offer.
A second full sales page: the buyer already trusts you; one gap, one offer, one price.
'Yes, upgrade me!' buttons that hide what is charged: say exactly what is added and for how much.
Decline wording like 'No, I don't want to succeed': it is confirm shaming under the CCPA guidelines and makes refunds more likely. Use 'No thanks, continue'.
Invented strike-through prices ('Rs 4,999 Rs 499') for something never sold at Rs 4,999: compare with a real price or drop the anchor.
Stacking three upsells in a row: one upsell and at most one downsell; then let them go.

ban.label: confirm-shaming decline
ban.regex: (?i)no,? i (don'?t|do not) want to (succeed|grow|save|earn)|i('?d| would) rather (stay|keep|waste)

cards.exemplar_brief: OTO page for a Bengaluru creator's Rs 1,999 'Excel for accountants' video course, shown right after payment: offer a Rs 699 pack of ready GST, payroll and invoice templates; English with light Hinglish; 150-250 words; confirmation bar, headline, gap, offer bullets, price, one yes button, neutral no-thanks link, and a Rs 299 downsell line (20 templates instead of the full pack); goal: add-on take rate.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. Confirmation bar first (order, amount, login email), headline ties the pack to the course, the gap is in the buyer's terms without knocking the course ('takes the very time you bought this course to save'), 4 outcome bullets, Rs 699 once with no second checkout, yes button names item and price, neutral 'No thanks, take me to my course', Rs 299 downsell with one line on the difference. No fake anchor, no timer, 247 words. Light Hinglish sits naturally. [N] template counts are fair placeholders (not supplied). Headline is serviceable rather than sharp.

cards.name: User guide / product manual
cards.summary: Task-based instructions that take a user from unboxing or sign-up to doing the job the product exists for. Good looks like chapters named after what the user wants to do, numbered steps with one action each and the expected result after it, warnings placed before the step they apply to, and terms that match the labels on the device or screen exactly.
use_for: Manuals and quick-start guides for appliances, electronics and tools
SaaS and app user guides organised by task
Bilingual English-Hindi (or regional language) manuals for the Indian market
In-box quick-start leaflets and setup cards
Admin guides for B2B software
avoid: One question answered on a help centre: use genre:knowledge_base_article
Diagnosing a specific fault: use genre:troubleshooting_guide
Developer-facing docs: use genre:api_reference or genre:developer_tutorial
Internal team procedures: use genre:sop_process_doc
Marketing claims inside the manual ('the best plug in India'): the user already bought it; keep to instructions
Feature tours ('The Settings menu contains...'): organise by task ('Change the Wi-Fi network')

cards.goal: The user completes the task the first time, without calling support or returning the product.

structure.does: Product name and model or app version, who the guide is for, and the conventions used (Note, Caution, Warning; bold for on-screen labels).

Hazards that apply throughout, with signal words (Warning = injury risk, Caution = damage risk). Statutory declarations the category requires come from the client's compliance owner; leave a marked placeholder, never invent them.
structure.length: Hardware: half to one page; software: usually none

structure.part: What's in the box / before you start
structure.does: Parts list matching the labelled diagram, and prerequisites (account, app, power, Wi-Fi band, tools).
The shortest path to first success, as numbered steps with the expected result.

One chapter per user goal, titled with a verb ('Schedule the plug to switch off'). Numbered steps, one action each, the UI or button label in bold exactly as printed, the result after each step ('The light turns blue').
Table of Problem, Likely cause, What to do, ordered by how often it happens.
Spec table copied from the engineering sheet, cleaning and storage, warranty terms from the client, support contacts.

length.note: Driven by the number of user tasks. A quick-start leaflet fits 300-600 words; a consumer appliance manual 2,000-6,000; B2B software guides run far longer and are split into separate guides by role. For the verify wave: quick start, one task chapter and troubleshooting (700-1,000 words).

checklist: Are chapters titled by user task (verb first), not by feature or menu?
Is every step numbered with exactly one action?
Does each step (or group of steps) say what the user should see afterwards?
Are warnings and cautions placed before the step they apply to?
Do on-screen and on-device labels appear exactly as printed, in bold?
Is one term used for one thing throughout (not 'plug', 'device' and 'unit' for the same object)?
Is there a quick start that reaches first success in 7 steps or fewer?
Is there a troubleshooting table with cause and fix for each problem?
Are all specifications, warranty terms and statutory lines from the client, with placeholders where missing?
pitfalls: Two actions in one step ('Open the app and tap Add device'): the user does the first and loses their place. Split them.
Warnings after the step ('Note: unplug before cleaning' at the end): by then the damage is done. Put it before step 1 of that task.
Feature-by-feature chapters copied from the menu structure: users arrive with a goal, so chapter titles must be goals.
Synonyms for variety: technical readers assume a new word means a new thing. Pick one term and keep it.
Invented specifications or certifications: copy from the spec sheet or leave [SPEC: rated load] for the client.
Screenshots described as 'the screen below': describe what to tap in words so the step works without the image (and for screen readers).
Translating word for word into Hindi: write the Hindi version for the reader, keeping on-device English labels as printed.
cards.exemplar_brief: Quick start, one task chapter and troubleshooting for the user guide of a Rs 1,499 Wi-Fi smart plug made by a Noida electronics brand, for first-time smart-home buyers in Tier-2 cities; plain English (Hindi version written separately); 700-1,000 words: what's in the box, app setup in numbered steps with expected results, the task 'Schedule the geyser to switch off', a troubleshooting table; specs and statutory lines as [placeholders]; goal: setup without calling support.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. About-this-guide conventions, safety warnings with signal words, box list, prerequisites, a 7-step quick start with the expected result after every step, a verb-titled task chapter ('Schedule the geyser to switch off') with warnings before step 1 (wattage vs [SPEC: rated load], wet-area socket), bold UI labels, one term ('the plug') throughout, an 8-row troubleshooting table ordered sensibly, statutory/spec/warranty lines as placeholders as the brief asks. 821 words. Nits: quick-start step 3 bundles two actions (create account + enter OTP) and step 11 ('Test it') compresses a repeat of steps 6-10 into one line.

cards.summary: The words inside an interface: buttons, labels, helper text, empty states, confirmations and success messages. Good looks like a string table where every line helps the user finish the task on that screen: verbs on buttons that say what happens, labels that match the user's vocabulary, helper text that prevents the error, and a consistent voice within each string's character limit.

Rewriting confusing screens that drive support tickets or drop-offs
Empty states, tooltips, toasts and confirmation dialogs
Chatbot quick-reply buttons and menu labels
Hindi or Hinglish UI strings alongside English for in-app language toggles
avoid: Error states as the main job: use genre:error_messages
Multi-screen first-run walkthroughs: use genre:onboarding_flow_copy
Push and in-app message campaigns: use genre:push_notification
Hero headlines and marketing pages: use genre:landing_page
Writing the voice rules for the whole product: use genre:brand_voice_guide
Jokes in moments of risk (payments, deletion, health data): be plain there

cards.goal: The user completes the task on the screen without hesitating, mis-tapping or contacting support.

structure.does: For each screen: name, the user's goal, the state covered (default, empty, loading, success, error) and any variables.
Rows of Element, Copy, Character limit, Notes (variables like {name}, plural forms, where truncation happens). This is the deliverable developers paste.
Verb plus object, front-loaded, naming the outcome ('Add nominee', 'Pay Rs 1,250'). Never 'Submit' or 'Click here'.
Label is a short noun the user would say; helper text gives the format or example that prevents the error ('As on your PAN card'); placeholders never carry required information.
structure.length: Label 1-4 words; helper text under about 12 words

structure.does: What will appear here, why it is empty now, and one action to fill it.
Title asks the specific question ('Remove Priya as nominee?'), body states the consequence, buttons repeat the verb ('Remove' / 'Keep nominee').
What happened in past tense plus the next step or Undo where possible.
One line per non-obvious choice, alternatives tried, and localisation flags (Hindi strings often run longer; check limits).

length.note: Total visible copy for the flow; the number of screens and states drives it. Each string is short; the rationale notes are extra and not counted against character limits.

checklist: Does every button start with a verb and name what will happen?
Is every string within its stated character limit, including the Hindi or Hinglish version?
Does every form field have a visible label (not just a placeholder)?
Does helper text prevent the most likely error on that field?
Does every destructive dialog name the object and repeat the verb on its button?
Is one term used for one concept across all screens?
Does every empty state offer one action?
Is the decline or cancel option worded neutrally, with no guilt?
Are variables and plural forms marked for developers?
pitfalls: 'Submit', 'OK' and 'Yes/No' buttons: the user must reread the question. Use the action: 'Save address', 'Delete 3 photos'.
Writing copy without the screen: you miss truncation, button width and state. Ask for the design file or a screenshot of each state.
Playful copy on a payment failure ('Oopsie!'): match tone to the user's stress; be direct and say what to do.
Placeholders as labels: they vanish when typing begins and fail screen readers. Keep a visible label.
Different words for the same thing ('nominee', 'beneficiary', 'family member'): users think they are different. Pick the one users say, and use it everywhere.
Machine-translated Hindi strings: 'जमा करें' for Submit on a payment screen confuses; have Hinglish or Hindi written for the screen and checked in context (lang:localization_qa).
Confirm-shaming opt-outs ('No, I don't care about security'): a listed dark pattern under the CCPA guidelines.
cards.exemplar_brief: Microcopy string table for the 'Add nominee' flow in a Mumbai mutual-fund investing app: 4 screens (empty state, nominee form with name, relationship, share percentage and date of birth, review-and-confirm, success), plus a destructive 'Remove nominee' dialog; English with a Hinglish column for the in-app language toggle; each string with a character limit and notes; goal: nominee added without a support ticket.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C2. A real developer-ready string table: per-screen goal, state and variables; Element/English/Hinglish/Limit/Notes columns; variable lengths declared and every English and Hinglish string fits its limit (re-checked by script). Buttons are verb+object, visible labels with helper text that prevents the likely error ('As on their PAN or Aadhaar', total-100% rule shown before the error), success in past tense with a conditional next step for shares under 100%, destructive dialog names the person and repeats the verb ('Remove' / 'Keep nominee'), one term ('nominee', 'share') throughout. Hinglish is natural aap-register and gender-neutral ('ab aapke nominee hain'). SEBI/fund-house rules (relationship list, minor guardian fields, no Undo) are flagged for compliance rather than asserted.

cards.name: Digital video ad script (YouTube, Reels, pre-roll)
cards.summary: A script for a paid online video ad with a fixed spot length, written so the brand and the one message land before the viewer can skip. Good looks like a two-column audio/visual script whose first five seconds carry a hook and the brand, that works with sound off through supers, and that ends on one CTA matched to the campaign goal, with cutdowns for shorter slots.
use_for: YouTube skippable in-stream ads (the first five seconds decide everything)
Six-second bumper ads and their cutdowns from a longer spot
Instagram and Facebook Reels and Stories ads made by the brand
OTT and publisher pre-roll
App-install and performance video with a hard CTA
avoid: Broadcast TV or connected-TV spots with broadcast code checks: use genre:tvc_script
A creator-filmed testimonial look: use genre:ugc_ad_script
A long persuasive video that sells on its own page: use genre:vsl_script
Organic reels and explainers: use genre:short_form_video_script or genre:explainer_video_script
Saving the brand name for the end card: viewers who skip at five seconds never see it

cards.goal: Even viewers who skip at five seconds remember the brand and one message, and the intended viewers take the one action (shop, install, book, search).

structure.does: Spot length (6, 15, 20 or 30 s), placement, aspect ratio (16:9 YouTube, 9:16 Reels/Shorts), campaign objective, sound-on or sound-off assumption, mandatory supers and disclaimers, the single message in one sentence.
A striking visual or line tied to the problem or desire, with the brand or product named or clearly shown before the skip point. Supers carry the hook for sound-off viewing.
One benefit shown, not listed: a demo, a before/after that is real, a customer moment. Every line of VO earns its seconds.
Spoken action plus on-screen CTA text, logo, offer or URL; matches the ad's button text.
A 6-second bumper (one idea, brand, product; no story) and a 15-second version, written as separate columns, not trimmed afterwards.
Headline, long headline, description and CTA text within the platform limits (plat:youtube_video_ads).

length.note: Spoken words per version, set by the spot length. Time each version by reading the VO aloud at the voice artist's pace and leave a beat of silence before the end card; Hindi VO often needs fewer words for the same seconds. Multiple cutdowns sit in one script.

checklist: Is the brand or product named or clearly shown within the first five seconds?
Does the opening work with sound off (supers or a self-explaining visual)?
Is there exactly one message, stated in one sentence in the spec header?
Is the script two-column (visual | audio) with timings?
Does each version fit its spot length when read aloud?
Does the CTA name one action that matches the campaign objective and button?
Is there a 6-second version written as its own idea, not a crop?
Are disclaimers in the same language as the claim and on screen long enough to read?
Are text assets within the platform character limits?
pitfalls: A slow brand film opening (sunrise, logo sting, music build): skippable viewers leave at five seconds. Open on the problem, product or face.
Three messages in thirty seconds: the viewer keeps none. Pick one; the others become separate variants.
VO that repeats what the picture already shows: let the visual carry it and use VO for what the eye cannot see (price, reason, feeling).
Disclaimers in tiny English under a Hindi VO: CCPA's misleading-ads guidelines want them in the same language and legible; budget screen time for them.
The 6-second bumper trimmed from the 30: it becomes a fragment. Write it as one complete thought with the brand.
Health or performance claims the brand cannot substantiate ('doubles hair growth'): state what the product is and does, and keep the proof the client holds.

require.label: has a spoken or on-screen CTA

cards.exemplar_brief: 30-second YouTube skippable in-stream ad plus a 6-second bumper for a Kochi Ayurvedic hair-oil brand launching online in North India; audience: women 25-40 in Delhi NCR; Hindi VO with English supers; two-column AV script with timings; brand and product shown before 5 seconds; no medical or growth claims; text assets within YouTube limits; goal: click 'Shop now' to the brand site.

verified.note: ROUND 2: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. New creative with a real insight: it opens on Maa's Sunday call ('Beta, tel lagaya?') and the white lie next to a sealed bottle. The bottle is in frame from 0:01 and the brand super lands at 0:02. The middle beat (she oils her own hair, 'das minute sirf apne naam') now matches its VO and super, and the second call pays it off ('is baar sach mein'). The end card has silence from 0:29 and a statutory slot. The bumper is its own idea (a bottle set on a circled Sunday). Text assets are 23/80/80/8 against 30/90/90/10 (re-checked), and there is no growth or treatment claim. Nits (writer): 'Made in Kochi' is supered at 0:02 and again at 0:13 with the VO, where once would do; the bumper's last 3 s stack three supers plus the statutory line, too many to read; the proof beat's ingredient line is a slot (fair: the brief gives none). | round 1: weak 7

cards.name: Video essay script
cards.summary: An argument-led long-form YouTube script that builds a thesis through narration, clips and evidence. Good looks like a cold open that raises a real question, a clear thesis by the end of the first minute or two, chapters that each add one piece of evidence and end on a turn, a fair treatment of the strongest counter-argument, and a conclusion that changes how the opening looks.
use_for: Analysis channels: film, business case studies, history, tech, cities, culture
Faceless channels built on narration, archive and graphics
Hindi and Hinglish deep-dive channels explaining Indian policy, brands or culture
Brand-funded documentary-style essays where the brand is a sponsor, not the subject
avoid: Breaking news and 'what we know so far': use genre:news_explainer
Presenter-personality videos where the host is the draw: use genre:youtube_video_script
Reacting to someone else's video: use genre:commentary_video_script
Interview-led documentaries: use genre:documentary_narration
Clips used as filler or entertainment: India's fair-dealing exception covers criticism, review and reporting, so every borrowed clip must be the thing you are analysing

sources.title: Upwork: 14 Types of Freelance Writing Jobs and What They Pay (published 2026-01-21)
sources.supports: script writer freelance rate band $30-$56 per hour

sources.title: Copyright Act, 1957 (India), s.52
sources.supports: fair dealing allowed for private use and research, criticism or review, and reporting current events; criticism/review use must carry an acknowledgment of the work

buyers: YouTube channel owners in analysis niches
Edtech and brands sponsoring long-form content
cards.value_why: Covered by Upwork's script writer type ($30-$56/hr, 2026-01-21) but with no separate category; most video essayists write their own, so commissioned work is occasional.
cards.goal: The viewer watches to the end, comes away convinced or rethinking, and comments or subscribes.

structure.does: A specific scene, clip, number or paradox that raises the question the essay answers. No channel intro.
The question in plain words, your answer (the thesis), why it matters to the viewer, and the chapters ahead.
Only what the viewer needs to follow the argument: definitions, a short timeline, the key players.

Each makes one claim, shows evidence (clip, data, document, quote with source), analyses it, and ends on a turn or open question that pulls into the next chapter. Mark [CLIP: title, timestamp, why], [GRAPHIC: ...] and [SOURCE: ...].
The strongest opposing view stated fairly, then your answer to it.
Return to the cold open with new meaning; what the thesis implies beyond this topic.
One ask (comment prompt or next video), sponsor mention if any with disclosure, sources in description.

length.note: Narration words; the depth of the argument and the amount of clip time drive it. Time by reading aloud, then add clip and pause time. For the verify wave: cold open, thesis and first chapter (1,000-1,400 words).

checklist: Does the cold open pose a specific question within the first 45 seconds?
Is the thesis stated in one sentence by the end of the first two minutes?
Does each chapter make one claim backed by named evidence?
Is every borrowed clip analysed or criticised, and acknowledged by title and creator?
Does each chapter end with a turn or question leading into the next?
Is the strongest counter-argument stated fairly before it is answered?
Does the conclusion call back to the cold open?
Is every factual claim sourced in the script notes?
Is the narration written for the ear (short sentences, no 'as shown above')?
pitfalls: A topic instead of a thesis ('a video about flyovers'): viewers stay for an argument. Write the claim you will prove in one sentence before outlining.
Clip-heavy summaries of a film or show with thin commentary: that is replay, not criticism, and weakens any fair-dealing defence. Show only what you analyse.
A strawman counter-argument: commenters will supply the real one. State the best version and answer it.
Chapters that are lists of facts: end each on a 'but' or 'which raises the question' so the next one is needed.
Unsourced numbers in a confident voice: put [SOURCE] notes in the script and the links in the description.
Allegations about named living people or companies beyond the public record: defamation risk under BNS s.356; attribute and source, or drop it.
cards.exemplar_brief: Cold open, thesis and first argument chapter (1,000-1,400 words) of a Hinglish video essay for a Lucknow analysis channel: 'Why every new flyover in Indian cities makes traffic worse' (induced demand); audience: urban viewers 18-35; narration in Roman-script Hinglish with [CLIP], [GRAPHIC] and [SOURCE] markers; no invented statistics (mark any number [SOURCE NEEDED]); goal: watch to the end and comment.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. Cold open poses the paradox (Day-1 empty flyover vs jam at 6 pm) inside 45 s; thesis in one line with stakes and a 4-chapter roadmap; short fair context that also previews the planners' counter-argument for ch. 4; chapter 1 makes one claim (cheaper trip time -> more trips) with four kinds of induced trips, cites Duranton & Turner, 'The Fundamental Law of Road Congestion', AER 2011 (real; the stated finding matches), marks Indian evidence and cost [SOURCE NEEDED], and ends on a turn into ch. 2 (the jam moves to the exit). Clip markers say why and credit. Ear-friendly analogies (free delivery, new fridge). Nit: register slides between 'aap ... kijiye' and 'aap kahoge / jaate ho', which a Lucknow audience will notice; pick one.

cards.name: Vlog outline / shoot plan
cards.summary: A one-page beat sheet for an unscripted vlog: the opening promise, the planned moments in order, questions to ask on camera, a plan B, and the ending that pays off the promise. Good looks like an outline that makes sure the creator comes back with a story and the B-roll to cut it, while leaving room for what actually happens.
use_for: Travel, food-walk and day-in-the-life vlogs
Brand or tourism-board sponsored visits that must cover certain points
Event and behind-the-scenes vlogs
Creator collaborations where two people need the same plan
Challenge vlogs ('one day on Rs 1,500')
avoid: To-camera explainers scripted line by line: use genre:talking_head_script
Fully scripted YouTube videos: use genre:youtube_video_script
The sponsor segment itself: use genre:sponsored_integration_script and drop it into the outline
Live streams: use genre:livestream_run_of_show
Full sentences for the creator to recite: write say-points as bullets so they sound natural

Brands, hotels and tourism boards sponsoring a vlog visit
cards.value_why: Creators usually write their own outlines and no marketplace category was found on 2026-10-04; paid work appears mainly when a sponsor or creator team needs a shoot plan.
cards.goal: The creator comes back with footage that cuts into a story (promise, moments, payoff) without sounding scripted, and the sponsor's points are covered.

structure.does: What the viewer gets or the question the vlog answers, plus the title and thumbnail idea it must deliver on.
2-3 cold-open lines to say on location, each with the shot (walking in, a reveal, a problem).
Beats in shooting order: place, what happens, why it matters to the story, say-points as bullets, B-roll to grab. Include a mid-video re-hook (a tracker, a countdown, a reveal).
Open questions for people met (vendors, guides, locals) that invite a story, not a yes/no.
What to shoot if a moment fails: closed shop, rain, no permission to film.
Where it sits, must-say points, disclosure wording and timing.
Payoff of the opening promise, 2 closing-line options, one CTA.
Establishing shots, details, transitions, the thumbnail frame, a selfie-angle reaction.

length.note: One to two pages; the number of locations and whether there is a sponsor drive it. Longer outlines get ignored on a shoot day.

checklist: Is the promise stated in one or two lines that the title could carry?
Are there at least two cold-open options shot on location?
Are planned moments in shooting order, each with a reason it matters to the story?
Are say-points bullets rather than full sentences?
Are there at least five open questions for people on camera?
Is there a plan B for the riskiest moment?
Does the ending pay off the opening promise?
If sponsored, are disclosure wording and placement written in?
pitfalls: A list of places with no story: give the day a question or a constraint (a budget, a dish to find, a person to meet) so moments build.
Opening with 'Hey guys, welcome back': the first seconds decide retention. Open on the problem or the most striking moment.
Scripted lines for strangers: you cannot script locals. Write questions that get stories ('Yahan sabse purana customer kaun hai?').
No B-roll list: the editor ends up with only talking footage. List the details and transitions to grab at each stop.
Free hotel stay mentioned casually with no disclosure: ASCI counts free stays and products as a material connection.
No plan B: when the main moment fails, the vlog has no spine. Note an alternative for each risky beat.

ban.label: stock vlog opener
ban.regex: (?i)hey guys,? welcome back|hello dosto,? welcome back

cards.exemplar_brief: Shoot outline for a Hinglish travel vlogger's 12-15 minute YouTube vlog 'Rs 1,500 mein Varanasi ka ek din' (one day in Varanasi on Rs 1,500); audience: student travellers; Hinglish (Roman); 300-500 words with the promise, two cold-open options, 6-8 planned moments with a running budget tracker, questions for a boatman and a chai seller, a rain plan B, ending and shot checklist; goal: a story the editor can cut.

verified.note: ROUND 2: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. Round-1 faults fixed: the re-hook matches the numbers (Rs 670 left for three things), feminine nouns take 'ki' ('aarti ki jagah'), every beat has a why, say-points and B-roll, and the questions use 'aap' throughout. The tracker reconciles (1,500 to 670, then 420 or 220 for the ride back). Two on-location cold opens, 7 beats in shooting order, 6 story-inviting questions, a rain and flood plan B with a safety line, a payoff with 2 closing lines and one CTA, and 10 shot ticks. The local detail is right (kachori-jalebi, BHU, tamatar chaat, baati-chokha). Nits (writer): by its own caps the day ends Rs 220-420 under budget, so 'raat tak budget bachega?' has little jeopardy; some say-points are only labels ('Say: final tracker', 'steps ya nao, kyun'). | round 1: weak 7

cards.name: VSL (video sales letter) script
cards.summary: A sales letter delivered as video, usually text on screen with voice-over: a hook, the problem, a story, the mechanism that explains why this works, proof, the offer, the guarantee and a close. Good looks like one idea per slide, short read-aloud lines, proof the seller can document, and a price and guarantee stated plainly before the final call to action.
use_for: Course, coaching and membership offers sold on a funnel page
High-ticket application funnels ('watch, then book a call')
Software and service offers to cold paid traffic
Short VSLs on upsell pages
Hindi and Hinglish VSLs for Indian course creators
avoid: Short paid ads that send people to the VSL: use genre:video_ad_script or genre:ugc_ad_script
A live teaching session that ends in a pitch: use genre:webinar_pitch_script
The written page around the video: use genre:sales_page or genre:landing_page
Income, job, cure or returns guarantees: CCPA guidelines (coaching, misleading ads) and SEBI rules for finance forbid them; sell the skill and the process
Fake scarcity and fake live counters: listed dark patterns

sources.supports: no guaranteed selection, job, salary or admission claims; successful-candidate testimonials need disclosed details and written consent

buyers: SaaS and service businesses selling to cold traffic
cards.value_why: Upwork runs a Video Sales Letter Specialists hire category, Fiverr a VSL-script gig tag, and AWAI prices 'Long-Form VSL Script' as its own project (harvest, 2026-10-04); a VSL is the conversion asset of a funnel, so buyers pay for it.
cards.goal: The viewer clicks the buy, enrol or apply button below the video.

structure.does: Calls out the viewer and opens with a promise, a story or a sharp problem, plus a reason to keep watching. No logo, no host introduction first.
The problem in the viewer's words and what it costs them in time, money, status; specific scenes, not adjectives.
How the founder or a customer found the answer; a turning point the viewer can see themselves in.
Why this works when what they tried failed: the named method, in plain cause-and-effect.
Testimonials with consent and real details, demos, documented results with their context; no invented numbers.
What they get (modules, support, bonuses), how it works, the price, and an honest comparison.
The refund or risk-reversal terms in plain words, matching the checkout.
Who it is for and not for, two or three objections answered, the CTA said and shown, a real deadline if one exists.

length.note: Price and awareness set length: a warm audience and a low price can buy from a 3-5 minute VSL; a cold audience and a high price may need 20-40 minutes (AWAI lists a long-form VSL). Write one idea per slide line; time by reading aloud.

checklist: Does the first 30 seconds call out the viewer and give a reason to keep watching?
Is each slide line one idea, short enough to read in one glance?
Is the mechanism explained as cause and effect, not just named?
Is every result or testimonial something the seller can document, with consent?
Are the price and what is included stated plainly?
Do the guarantee terms match the checkout and refund policy?
Are there no guaranteed income, job, cure or returns claims?
Is the CTA said and shown, pointing to the button below the video?
Is any deadline or limit real?
pitfalls: A 5-minute origin story before the viewer knows what is in it for them: lead with the problem or promise, tell the story once they care.
Paragraph slides: a VSL is read on screen. One line per slide, a sentence break at every breath.
'Secret' mechanisms that are just the product name: explain why it works in two or three cause-and-effect steps.

Screenshots of student earnings as proof: for coaching, CCPA bars success claims without disclosed details and consent; for money topics SEBI and ASCI rules bite. Show the skill outcome (portfolio, fluency, certificate) instead.
Hiding the price until after 'but wait, there's more': state it plainly with what is included; drip-feeding charges later is a listed dark pattern.
Copy-pasting a US template: translate the stakes, prices and examples into the viewer's world (Rs, local job titles, Hinglish phrasing).
cards.exemplar_brief: 12-15 minute text-on-screen VSL (1,800-2,200 words) for a Hyderabad spoken-English coaching programme for IT support staff moving into client-facing roles; Rs 6,999 for 8 weeks with a 7-day refund; audience: 24-32-year-olds in Tier-2 cities, comfortable in Hinglish; English VO with Hinglish lines where natural, one line per slide; no salary or job guarantees (CCPA coaching guidelines); goal: click 'Enrol now' below the video.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. One line per slide, viewer called out in the first lines with a reason to stay; problem told as a scene (the Tuesday call, 'Sir, actually, the server, it was, like, down'); story with marked true-fact slots for the founder; mechanism explained as cause and effect (live speech needs ready sentence beginnings -> missing client phrases -> blank), with Call Frames / Three-Beat Reply and before/after lines; proof as consented placeholders with an explicit no-promotion/no-salary/no-job promise (CCPA coaching-compliant); price, inclusions, 'under Rs 875 a week' (6,999/8 = 874.9, correct), 7-day refund, no fake deadline; CTA said and shown. Hinglish lines land ('Samajh sab aata hai. Bolna nahi aata.'). Nits: 'Three questions I hear a lot' is followed by four; saying the audience's age range ('aged 24 to 32') on screen reads like the brief leaking into copy.

Episodes written inside a writers' room from an approved outline
YouTube and branded web series with recurring characters
Regional-language and Hindi series with English action lines

A standalone film: use genre:screenplay_feature
The series pitch, world and season arc: use genre:worldbuilding_bible, genre:synopsis or genre:film_treatment
Audio-only series: use genre:audio_series_script
Writing episode 1 as all setup: the pilot must also deliver a complete, satisfying episode

structure.does: Series title, episode number and title, 'Written by', draft and date, contact.
A scene that hooks: a question, a danger or a comic disaster that defines the episode, before the titles.
Establishes the A-plot problem for this episode and introduces the B-plot; ends on a turn that commits the lead.
structure.length: About a quarter of the pages

structure.does: Complications that escalate; a midpoint shift; the B-plot crosses the A-plot and raises its stakes.
The A-plot resolves through the lead's choice; the B-plot resolves or deepens; a series-arc thread moves forward.
structure.length: About a quarter of the pages

structure.does: A reveal, cliffhanger or emotional sting that pulls into the next episode.
INT./EXT. LOCATION - DAY/NIGHT heading, present-tense action of what is seen and heard, character cue in capitals above dialogue; each scene changes something.

length.note: Pages in standard screenplay format, at roughly a page per minute: write to the runtime the platform names (half-hour comedy and hour-long drama differ). For the verify wave: cold open and act one (8-10 pages, about 1,500-2,000 words).

checklist: Does the cold open hook within the first two pages?
Is there a clear A-plot problem for this episode, separate from the season arc?
Is there a B-plot that crosses the A-plot at least once?
Does every scene start with an INT./EXT. heading and end with something changed?
Is action in present tense and limited to what can be seen or heard?
Does the A-plot resolve through the lead's own choice?
Does the episode end on a hook into the next one?
Does the page count fit the runtime at about a page a minute?
Is each main character's voice distinct enough to identify without the cue?
pitfalls: A pilot that only sets up the world: platforms buy episodes that work. Give episode 1 its own problem and payoff, and let the world show through it.
Cliffhanger by withholding (a character 'sees something' and we cut): it feels cheap. End on a reveal or a decision that changes the next episode.
Exposition dialogue about backstory ('As you know, since Papa died...'): show it in behaviour or a prop and trust the viewer.
Every scene in the same two locations with talking only: give scenes an action and a place that adds conflict.
Real, living people or businesses with invented scandal: defamation risk under BNS s.356; fictionalise names and facts.
Sharing the script before registering or dating drafts: register with SWA (members) or keep dated versions.
cards.exemplar_brief: Cold open and act one (8-10 pages, about 1,500-2,000 words) of the pilot of a 6-episode Hindi OTT comedy-drama: three siblings in Indore must run their late father's failing sweet shop through one Diwali season to inherit it; scene headings and action in English, dialogue in Roman-script Hindi; establish the A-plot (the shop's first big order), the B-plot (the eldest sister's secret job offer in Pune) and end act one on a turn.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V1 C1. A cold open that hooks on page one (stuck shutter, jalebi that becomes 'a brown map of Madhya Pradesh', Sharma ji's bucket killing the live stream) and the will's condition as the clock; A-plot (Khanna's 300 boxes, recipe pages torn out) and B-plot (Anjali's Pune offer) both planted and crossed; act one ends on a strong double turn (yes to the order, 'I accept' to Pune in the same breath); proper INT./EXT. headings, present-tense action, distinct voices (Bhura Kaka's Malwi is a nice touch). Writer fault on the brief: dialogue was to be Roman-script Hindi, but more than half is English (the whole cold-open exchange, Vakil Trivedi, Jagdish Chacha, the back-office scene, Ritu), so a Hindi OTT needs a dialogue pass before it goes out.

Coaching and membership launches run as a live event
Evergreen automated webinars feeding a course
SaaS demo webinars ending in a trial or annual-plan offer
Workshop-to-cohort conversions for professional skills

A recorded sales video watched alone: use genre:vsl_script
The registration page and reminder emails: use genre:landing_page and genre:email_sequence_nurture

Guaranteed income, job, selection or returns: CCPA's coaching guidelines bar them, and SEBI rules restrict market 'education' that tips or promises returns
