sources.title: CCPA Guidelines for Prevention of Misleading Advertisement in Coaching Sector, 2024
sources.supports: no false success-rate claims or guaranteed selection, job, salary or admission; no false urgency; topper testimonials need consent and disclosed details

cards.value_why: AWAI prices 'Teleseminar/Webinar Script' as its own project (2026-02-02) and Upwork funnel-copywriter listings include webinar scripts; in India the free-masterclass funnel is a standard course-creator and edtech format (harvest note).
cards.goal: Attendees stay to the offer and buy or apply during the session or before the real deadline that follows it.

structure.does: Who the session is for, the specific win they will have by the end, why to stay to the end (only if something real happens there), housekeeping: chat, replay, timing.
The host's own struggle with the same problem and the turning point; short and specific, connected to the attendee.

Usually three. Each teaches one real step and, in doing so, breaks one false belief that would stop a purchase (about the method, about the attendee's ability, about outside obstacles). Belief, story, proof, takeaway.
Recap the wins, ask permission to share the offer, name the gap between knowing and doing.
What the programme is, each component and what it does for them, bonuses, price, payment options, guarantee, deadline if real.
Answer the real objections (time, money, 'will it work for me'), repeat the link and price, chat prompts to type a word if they joined, end on time.

length.note: A 45-90 minute session read at a natural pace; the depth of teaching and the price of the offer drive it. Hindi and Hinglish hosts may speak slower; time a sample. For the verify wave: transition, offer and close (1,500-2,000 words).

checklist: Does the opening state a specific win the attendee will have by the end?
Does each teaching block teach a usable step, not just tease one?
Does each teaching block remove one named doubt about buying?
Does the transition ask permission before pitching?
Are price, inclusions, payment options and guarantee all stated?
Is any deadline, seat limit or bonus expiry real?
Are there no guaranteed income, job, selection or returns claims?
Are at least three real objections answered in the close or Q&A?
Is the purchase link repeated with what to do next?
pitfalls: Teaching that withholds everything ('I'll show you the how inside the course'): attendees feel tricked and leave before the offer. Give one complete, usable step per block.
A 20-minute origin story: keep the host story under about seven minutes and tie it to the attendee's problem.
Price revealed with a long fake 'value' stack (Rs 2,00,000 of value for Rs 4,999): anchor only on real alternatives (a tutor's fee, a classroom course).
'Only 5 seats left' when seats are unlimited: false scarcity is a listed dark pattern and CCPA's coaching guidelines bar false urgency.
Student income screenshots as proof: coaching guidelines require disclosed details and written consent; prefer skill outcomes and process.
Ignoring the chat: write moderator prompts and seeded questions so the live session has energy and the objections get voiced.
cards.exemplar_brief: Transition, offer and close (1,500-2,000 words) of a free 90-minute Sunday masterclass 'Bake your first eggless cake at home' by a Kolkata home-baking teacher, converting to a Rs 2,999 four-week online baking course with recorded lessons, weekly live doubt sessions and a recipe book; enrolment closes Sunday midnight (real), 7-day refund; Hinglish (Roman); goal: enrol during the live.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V1 C2. Transition recaps three wins, says the free value is theirs before selling, names the knowing-doing gap, asks permission with a chat 'haan'; offer stack is honest (week-by-week, recorded lessons, weekly live doubt session, recipe book, 'no bonus that isn't on screen', no inflated value stack, real-alternative anchor as placeholders); price, payment options, 7-day refund and the real Sunday-midnight close with a [reason] slot; seven objections answered including income (no earnings promise, FSSAI registration flagged [verify]); link repeated with what happens next; moderator and chat cues throughout. Writer fault, Hinglish slips: the female host says 'Jo dikha raha hoon' (rahi), 'Dahi aur baking soda ka jodi' (ki), 'Jaanna aur karna ke beech' (jaanne aur karne).

cards.name: Educational webinar / workshop script
cards.summary: Script and slide talking points for a teaching webinar or workshop: a promise, an agenda, teaching blocks with examples and audience check-ins, live Q&A prompts, a recap and one soft next step. Good looks like attendees being able to do one specific thing afterwards, speaker notes written for speaking, and interaction planned rather than hoped for.
use_for: B2B education webinars that build trust before any sale
Professional update sessions (tax, labour law, compliance changes) for clients
Customer training and product how-to sessions
L&D and HR workshops inside companies
NGO and government-scheme awareness sessions
avoid: A session whose real job is to sell a course or programme: use genre:webinar_pitch_script
Self-paced recorded lessons: use genre:course_lesson_script or genre:elearning_course_script
A one-speaker inspirational talk: use genre:keynote_speech or genre:ted_style_talk
Reading slides aloud: slides carry a few words; the script carries the explanation and examples

sources.title: Upwork: 14 Types of Freelance Writing Jobs and What They Pay (published 2026-01-21)
sources.supports: script writer freelance rate band $30-$56 per hour; instructional design listed among writing job types

cards.value_why: Covered by Upwork's script writer ($30-$56/hr) and instructional designer types (2026-01-21) with no webinar-specific category; usually bought inside an event or content retainer.
cards.goal: Attendees can do one specific thing after the session and take the one soft next step (download, trial, follow-up call).

structure.does: Welcome as people join, how to ask questions, whether a recording will be shared, a warm-up poll.
The one outcome, 3-4 agenda items, speaker credentials in one or two lines each.

3-4 blocks. Each: the concept in plain words, an example from the audience's world, a demo or worked case, a check-in (poll or 'type yes in chat if...'). Slide talking points as short bullets, speaker notes as spoken sentences.
Moderator lines, 3-5 seeded questions in case the chat is quiet, how to handle off-topic questions.
Three takeaways, each an action.
One resource or action (template, checklist, trial, consultation), how to get it, thanks.

length.note: A 30-60 minute session, including Q&A time that is not scripted word for word. Time a sample at the speaker's pace. For the verify wave: full outline plus one teaching block written out (1,000-1,400 words).

checklist: Is the outcome stated as something attendees will be able to do?
Is there an agenda with 3-4 items that the body follows?
Does each teaching block include an example from the audience's own context?
Is there at least one poll or chat check-in per teaching block?
Are slide bullets short and speaker notes written as spoken sentences?
Are there seeded Q&A questions for a quiet chat?
Does the recap give three action takeaways?
Is there exactly one next step, with no hard sell?
pitfalls: Ten minutes of company introduction: attendees came for the topic. Keep credentials to two lines and the company to the last slide.
Slides full of sentences the speaker reads out: put 3-6 words on the slide and the explanation in the notes.
Examples from another country's rules or market: use Indian forms, rupee figures and local cases where the audience is Indian.
No planned interaction: online attention drifts fast. Script a poll or chat prompt in every block.
A pitch hidden at the end of an 'educational' session: if there is an offer, it is a genre:webinar_pitch_script and should be honest about it.
Collecting attendee phone numbers 'for the certificate' and then marketing to them: purpose-specific consent applies under the DPDP regime.
cards.exemplar_brief: 45-minute educational webinar for a Pune HR-tech SaaS: 'Writing appraisal feedback that does not demotivate', for HR managers at 50-500-person Indian companies; English; full outline with agenda, three teaching blocks with slide talking points, two polls, Q&A seed questions, recap and a soft next step (download the feedback template); block one written out in full (1,000-1,400 words); goal: attendees rewrite one feedback note during the session.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. Outcome stated as a doing ('rewrite one real feedback note'), timed run of show matching a 3-item agenda, two polls, block one written out (~1,070 words) with Indian-context examples (150-person Pune services firm, 'the most loved label in Indian appraisals'), a camera test, two traps, a chat check-in and a 4-minute silent rewrite that delivers the session goal; blocks 2-3 as slide bullets plus notes; 5 seeded questions and an off-topic line; three action takeaways; one free template, no pitch. Nits: the 'After' examples are passive and drop the 'who' that the camera test itself demands; block 3 notes run host lines into the notes paragraph.

cards.name: Wedding / event invitation wording
cards.summary: The text of an Indian wedding card or e-invite: invocation, blessings, hosts, the couple, ceremonies with dates and times, venue and RSVP. Good looks like the family's tradition and protocol followed exactly, every name and relationship confirmed by the family, every date, day and time consistent, and a bilingual layout where both languages say the same thing.
use_for: Printed wedding cards (shaadi card matter) and inserts for each ceremony
WhatsApp e-invites, PDF invites and video invite captions
Reception, engagement, griha pravesh, mundan and other family functions
Bilingual Hindi-English or regional language-English cards
RSVP and 'with best compliments' lines for card printers
avoid: A birthday or anniversary wish: use genre:greeting_wishes_message
Promoting a ticketed or public event: use genre:event_promotion
The speech at the sangeet or reception: use genre:wedding_speech
Guessing names, relationships, gotras or spellings: leave [placeholders] and have the family confirm every one
Applying one religion's invocation to every family: ask what the family uses (or none)
buyers: Families, usually through a card printer or e-invite designer
Card printing shops that bundle wording
cards.value_why: Card printers and e-invite apps bundle the wording into the design price, so the standalone market is small (harvest note, 2026-10-04).
cards.goal: Every guest knows who is inviting them, to which functions, when and where, and how to RSVP; the family feels its elders were honoured in the right order.

structure.does: The family's chosen opening: for many Hindu families a deity line such as '॥ श्री गणेशाय नमः ॥'; Jain, Sikh, Muslim, Christian and other families have their own openings, and some use none. Ask.
Elders under whose blessings the wedding happens (grandparents, sometimes late elders with a respectful prefix the family chooses).
Names of the inviting parents and the invitation line ('request the pleasure of your company', 'सादर आमंत्रित करते हैं').
Bride's and groom's names with 'son of / daughter of' lines and the families' cities, in the order the hosting family uses.
Each function: name, date, day, time, venue if different, dress code if any. Dates and days must agree.
Full venue name, address, landmark and map link for e-invites.
RSVP names and numbers; lines such as 'स्वागतोत्सुक' or 'दर्शनाभिलाषी' listing family members eager to welcome guests.
'With best compliments from' and the family list; optionally the children's line ('Mere chachu ki shaadi mein zaroor aana').

length.note: Per language. The number of functions and the size of the family lists drive it; e-invites can split into one screen per function.

checklist: Is the invocation the one the family asked for (or omitted if they asked for none)?
Are elders, hosts and the couple in the order the family specified?
Is every name, relationship and city either supplied by the family or a clearly marked [placeholder]?
Does each ceremony have a name, date, day and time?
Do every date and weekday agree with each other?
Are the Hindi and English versions saying the same thing, with no missing ceremony?
Is there an RSVP line with at least one contact?
Are the venue name and address complete, with a map link on e-invites?
pitfalls: A wrong weekday next to a date: guests trust the day and come wrong. Check every date against a calendar.
Misspelt names or a relative left out of the list: a classic cause of family arguments and reprints. Send a proof list to the family before layout.
Translating English wording literally into Hindi ('आपकी कंपनी का अनुरोध करते हैं'): write the Hindi in the register families use ('सादर आमंत्रित').
Mixing number formats (2:00 PM, शाम 7 बजे, 19.30 hrs) on one card: pick one style per language and keep it.
Sanskrit invocations typed with broken conjuncts or wrong matras: use proper Unicode Devanagari and proofread at print size.
Copying a famous couple's invite text or a printer's template word for word: write for this family's functions and voice.

require.label: has dates or times in numerals
has an RSVP or contact line

cards.exemplar_brief: Bilingual (Hindi Devanagari and English) wedding card text for a Marwari family in Jodhpur: invocation, grandparents' blessings, hosts, the couple with parents, four functions (Ganesh puja, mehendi, sangeet, wedding with baraat swagat) with dates, days and times, venue, RSVP with two contacts and a 'with best compliments' line; every name, date and venue as a clear [placeholder]; 150-250 words per language; goal: guests know where to be and when.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp1 V2 C1. Both versions carry the same eight parts in the same order: Ganesh invocation, grandparents' blessings, hosts' invitation in the right register ('सपरिवार सादर आमंत्रित करते हैं'), the couple with parents and cities (आयुष्मती सौभाग्यकांक्षिणी / चिरंजीव), four functions each with date, day, time and venue slots, venue with landmark and map link, RSVP with two contacts, स्वागतोत्सुक / दर्शनाभिलाषी and a compliments line; every fact a clear placeholder as briefed; ~180-200 words per language. Correct and clean, but nothing makes it a Marwari Jodhpur card beyond the city name (no Rajasthani welcome line or family-voice touch), and the English is stiff ('Revered Grandfather Shri ... and Grandmother Smt.').

cards.name: Wedding speech / toast
cards.summary: A short, personal speech at a wedding, sangeet or reception that honours the couple and gets laughs without embarrassing anyone. Good looks like one or two specific stories that show who the person is, a warm welcome to the other family, jokes a grandmother and a college friend can both enjoy, and a toast or wish that lands in one clear line.
use_for: Best-man, maid-of-honour, sibling and friend speeches
Parent of the bride or groom speeches
Sangeet speeches and short Hinglish toasts
The couple's thank-you speech at the reception
Mixed-culture and NRI weddings with guests from several regions
avoid: Hosting the whole programme: use genre:anchoring_script
A formal welcome to dignitaries at an institutional event: use genre:welcome_address_vote_of_thanks
Roast material (exes, drinking, past mistakes): mixed-generation Indian audiences turn on the speaker; tease kindly about harmless habits
Reading a list of adjectives ('kind, caring, loyal'): tell the story that proves one of them

sources.title: Fiverr Writing & Translation: Speechwriting
sources.supports: speechwriting category covers personal speeches

buyers: Siblings, friends and parents of the couple (one-off personal commissions)
Wedding planners offering speech help as an add-on
Couples preparing their own thank-you speech
cards.value_why: A one-off personal commission sold through speechwriting marketplaces (Fiverr Speechwriting); low ticket size and no repeat buyer.
cards.goal: The couple feels seen, the room laughs at least once and joins the toast or applause at the end, and no one is embarrassed.

structure.does: Who you are and how you know the couple, with a light, self-aware line. No 'for those who don't know me' monologue.
One specific story that shows a quality of the bride or groom; concrete place, time, detail.
When you met them or knew they were right; a warm, specific welcome to the partner and their family (a line in their language if the family supplies it).
One observation about how they are as a couple, ideally a callback to the opening story.
A heartfelt line, then invite everyone to raise a glass or clap, naming the couple.

length.note: A few minutes when spoken; the slot the family gives and how many other speakers there are set it. Read it aloud with a timer, then cut. Shorter is almost always better at a sangeet with music waiting.

checklist: Does the opener say who the speaker is in one or two lines?
Is there at least one specific story with a time, place and detail?
Does the speech welcome the partner and their family by name?
Is every joke one the couple's grandparents could hear without discomfort?
Is there no mention of exes, drunken nights, or anything said in confidence?
Does the ending invite a toast or applause and name the couple?
Does it fit the time slot when read aloud?
Are sentences short enough to say in one breath?
pitfalls: Inside jokes only five friends understand: the rest of the room goes quiet. Set up every story so a stranger gets it.
Ex stories, drinking stories, 'he was such a player': the parents remember it for years. Tease about harmless quirks (always late, obsessed with cricket stats).
Making it about the speaker ('I remember when I...'): every story must end on the couple.
Dictionary-definition openers and quotes copied from the internet: open with your own moment instead.
Forgetting the other family: a line of welcome to them, by name, matters more than a third joke.
Hinglish written as formal Hindi on paper: write how the speaker actually talks and practise it aloud.
cards.exemplar_brief: Sangeet speech by the groom's younger sister at a Delhi Punjabi wedding; the groom is a quiet software engineer, the bride a Chennai-born doctor; mixed audience of grandparents and college friends, some Tamil-speaking; Hinglish with one welcome line in Tamil left as a [placeholder] for the family to supply; 3-4 minutes (450-600 words); one embarrassing-but-kind story, a welcome to the bride's family, closing toast; goal: laughs and a standing clap at the end.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V1 C1. Right shape for a sangeet: quick self-intro with a good opening joke (three minutes vs Veerji's three years of talking), one kind-embarrassing story with detail (the one-word 'Ok' on a 140-person family group), a warm turn (singing Dadi ji's song), the bride's family welcomed with the Tamil line left as briefed, a food callback, a toast that names the couple, nothing about exes or drinking, 507 words. Writer fault: Hinglish slips at the emotional beat ('maine ... gaana sunaai diya' is ungrammatical; 'sarson ka saag ke liye' should be 'ke saag'); the bride's family is welcomed as 'Chennai se aaye mehmaan', not by name (card checklist); the close sets up 'ek hi word kaafi hai, mere saath bolo' but then pays off with 'Cheers! Chak de phatte!' instead of the 'Ok' callback, so the last laugh is lost.

cards.name: Welcome address / vote of thanks
cards.summary: The formal opening and closing speeches at Indian institutional events, honouring dignitaries in protocol order. Good looks like exact names and designations, a protocol order agreed with the organisers, one line of genuine relevance for each guest instead of a biography, the event's purpose said in a few sentences, and a vote of thanks that refers to what was actually said on the day.
use_for: College and school functions (annual day, convocation, seminars)
Government programme launches and district-level events
Corporate conferences, AGMs and award nights
NGO, association and Hindi Pakhwada events
Bilingual events where the welcome is in Hindi and the thanks in English (or the reverse)
avoid: Linking every programme item through the event: use genre:anchoring_script
The main talk of the event: use genre:keynote_speech
Reading each guest's full CV: one line of relevance each, the rest belongs in the anchor's introduction
Guessing a designation or the order of dignitaries: confirm with the organisers' protocol list
buyers: Event organisers at colleges, schools and universities
PR and protocol teams for government events
cards.value_why: Ubiquitous at Indian institutional events but usually written in-house by staff or the anchor; little paid market (harvest note, 2026-10-04).
cards.goal: Every dignitary feels correctly honoured by name and designation, the audience knows why the event matters, and the programme starts and ends on time.

structure.does: Address dignitaries in the agreed protocol order: typically chief guest, guest of honour, presiding officer, other dignitaries on the dais, organisers, then the audience. Hindi-medium functions often address the अध्यक्ष (presiding officer) first, so follow the organisers' printed list rather than a default.
Name, exact designation, one line on why their presence matters to this event, an invitation to applaud.
The occasion, theme and what the audience will take away.
A collective welcome and a hand-over to the programme.

structure.part: Vote of thanks: chief guest and speakers
structure.does: Thank each by name for something specific they said or did today (written as a placeholder to fill live).

structure.part: Vote of thanks: everyone who made it happen
structure.does: Organisers, sponsors, staff, volunteers, technical and media teams, the audience, by group.
A short closing wish; announce the national anthem or next item only if it is on the programme.

length.note: Per speech. Short is the norm; the number of dignitaries drives length. Organisers usually give each speech a few minutes; time it aloud.

checklist: Are dignitaries addressed in the protocol order the organisers gave?
Is every name and designation exact, or a marked [placeholder] to confirm?
Does each dignitary get one line of relevance rather than a biography?
Is the event's purpose stated in four sentences or fewer?
Does the vote of thanks refer to at least one specific thing said or done during the event?
Are the support teams (volunteers, staff, technical, media) thanked?
Is it within the time slot when read aloud?
Is it free of stock phrases like 'last but not the least'?
pitfalls: A wrong or outdated designation ('Collector' for a District Magistrate who has moved): confirm the protocol list on the morning of the event.
Thanking the chief guest for 'his enlightening speech' with nothing specific: leave a [QUOTE FROM SPEECH] slot and fill it live.
Five-minute biographies of each guest: the anchor introduces; the welcome honours. One line each.
Forgetting the people who did the work (peons, volunteers, AV team): name the groups; it is what the staff remember.
Ornate filler ('words fall short to express our gratitude'): say thank you and say for what.
Mixing Hindi registers (Sanskritised in one line, colloquial in the next): pick a formal, clear register and keep it.
cards.exemplar_brief: Welcome address and vote of thanks (two pieces, 250-400 words each) for a district-level Swachhata awareness programme at a government college in Gaya, Bihar; chief guest: the District Magistrate, guest of honour: the college principal, presiding: a university nominee (all names as [placeholders]); formal Hindi in Devanagari; salutation order in both speeches exactly as on the organisers' printed list (demo): 1. अध्यक्ष (the presiding university nominee), 2. मुख्य अतिथि (the District Magistrate, printed as 'जिला पदाधिकारी'), 3. विशिष्ट अतिथि (the college principal), 4. मंच पर विराजमान अन्य गणमान्य अतिथि, 5. आयोजक एवं शिक्षकगण, 6. छात्र-छात्राएँ; the vote of thanks leaves a [placeholder] for one line quoted from the chief guest's speech; goal: every dignitary correctly honoured and the event on time.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp1 V2 C2. Two clean formal-Hindi pieces (~320 and ~314 words): salutation in the briefed order with correct vocatives ('साथियो', 'विद्यार्थियो'), one relevance line and an applause cue per dignitary, purpose in four sentences, hand-over to the anchor; vote of thanks with a fill-live quote slot for the DM and a slot for the principal, then organisers, volunteers, non-teaching staff, sound/tech team, media and students thanked by group; conditional anthem line; no stock cliches; consistent register. Nits: the presiding officer gets a generic thanks with no slot for something they said; 'कर रहे' is fixed masculine while the name slot offers श्री/श्रीमती; Bihar usage prints the DM as 'जिला पदाधिकारी', so confirm the designation. CARD FIX: exemplar_brief -> state the salutation order (it says 'exact protocol order' but gives none); structure[0].does -> add that Hindi-medium functions often address the अध्यक्ष (presiding officer) first, so follow the organisers' printed list rather than a default. | CARD FIXED 2026-10-07 (fix_genre_d): exemplar_brief now states the salutation order (organisers' printed list, demo); structure[0] notes that Hindi-medium functions often address the अध्यक्ष first, follow the printed list; re-judge pending.

cards.name: Welcome email series
cards.summary: The automated emails sent right after someone signs up, which deliver what was promised, set expectations and move the new subscriber to a first action. Good looks like email one arriving at once with the code or download, each later email doing one job (story, how to choose, proof, objection), one CTA per email, and a sender and tone that feel like a person.
use_for: D2C newsletter sign-ups with a first-order discount
Lead-magnet downloads that need follow-up
Creator and paid-newsletter welcome sequences
Edtech and course lead nurture after a free resource
B2B newsletter subscribers who need context before any sales talk
avoid: Getting a new user to activate product features: use genre:saas_onboarding_email
Long-cycle nurture after the welcome period: use genre:email_sequence_nurture
Order confirmations and receipts: use genre:transactional_email
One-off sale emails: use genre:promotional_email
Adding people who never opted in (bought lists, event attendees): consent rules and deliverability both punish it

sources.title: Klaviyo Help: Getting started with flows (updated 2026-03-30)
sources.supports: recommends building the welcome series first among flows (with abandoned cart, post-purchase and winback); separate email and SMS welcome flows

sources.supports: 1782 gigs on 2026-10-04; email-type filter lists Welcome emails

sources.title: Upwork In-Demand Skills 2026 (2026-02-04)
sources.supports: Email Marketing and Marketing Automation are among the top-10 most in-demand Sales & Marketing skills

sources.title: FTC: CAN-SPAM Act compliance guide
sources.supports: accurate subject lines, physical postal address, working opt-out (for US recipients)

buyers: D2C brands on Shopify and Klaviyo
cards.value_why: Klaviyo names the welcome series among the first flows to build (2026-03-30), Fiverr Email Copy (1782 gigs) has a Welcome emails filter, and Upwork's In-Demand Skills 2026 puts Email Marketing and Marketing Automation in the top 10 Sales & Marketing skills.
cards.goal: The new subscriber opens, gets what they signed up for, and takes one first action (first order, first use, a reply).

structure.does: The code, download or access link above the fold; what they will receive and how often; one CTA.
The founder's reason or the brand's point of difference, told as a short story with one concrete detail.

structure.part: Email 3: help them choose or start
structure.does: Best-sellers, a quick guide to picking the right variant, or a first-win tip.
Real reviews, the most common doubt answered (price, quality, returns, delivery time), the policy in plain words.
Reminder of the offer's real expiry or a simple question inviting a reply; preferences link.
Subject line, preview text, one CTA, sender name, footer with postal address and unsubscribe. Gaps between emails follow the buying cycle; a day or two apart is a common start.
structure.length: Subject within the limits in plat:email_subject_line

length.note: Whole series, usually 3-5 emails. Low-price impulse products need fewer, shorter emails; considered purchases and B2B need more education per email.

checklist: Does email 1 deliver the promised code or resource in its first lines?
Does email 1 say what the subscriber will receive and how often?
Does each email have a subject line and preview text that work as a pair?
Does each email have exactly one primary CTA?
Does each email do a different job (deliver, story, choose, proof, close)?
Is every review or claim one the brand can show?
Is any offer expiry real and the same across emails?
Does every email have an unsubscribe line and the sender's postal address?
pitfalls: Email 1 that opens with a long brand story before the code: the subscriber came for the code. Put it first.
Every email a discount reminder: the series teaches them to wait for sales. Give story, help and proof; mention the offer once or twice.
Subject lines that hide the content ('You won't believe this'): CAN-SPAM requires accurate subjects for US recipients and Indian inboxes punish spammy patterns.
Three CTAs per email (shop, follow, download app): pick one.
A 'no-reply' sender: invite replies in email 1 and read them; replies also help deliverability.
Treating a newsletter sign-up as consent for WhatsApp and SMS too: consent is purpose-specific; ask separately.

ban.label: spam-trigger phrases
ban.regex: (?i)\b(act now|click here|100% free|you have been selected|winner)\b

cards.exemplar_brief: 4-email welcome series for a Coimbatore D2C brand of cold-pressed cooking oils, triggered by a 10%-off newsletter sign-up; audience: home cooks aged 28-50 in South Indian metros; English; each email with subject, preview text, an 80-180-word body, one CTA and an unsubscribe line; email 1 delivers the code, email 4 answers 'why pay more than supermarket oil' with claims the brand can prove; goal: first order within 10 days.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. Four emails, each a different job (deliver, why us, choose, proof), each with subject + preview working as a pair, one CTA, sender name and a footer with postal address and unsubscribe; email 1 puts the code first and says what comes next and how often; send gaps day 0/2/4/6 fit the 10-day goal; email 3's oil-by-dish guide is authentic South Indian use (gingelly for podi and pickles, groundnut for dosa) with a first-win tip; email 4 answers the supermarket-price doubt with three provable items and a per-day cost to compute, and no health claims; expiry the same in all four. Bodies 92-163 words. Email 2's story is almost all placeholder (none supplied), so 'why us' cannot yet carry its weight.

cards.name: WhatsApp marketing broadcast / template message
cards.summary: A Meta-approved WhatsApp Business template sent to customers who opted in: offers, reminders, back-in-stock and re-engagement. Good looks like a message that reads like a note from a shop the customer knows, says why it arrived now, gives one specific offer with its end date, carries one button, and offers an easy way to stop, all inside the template's component limits.
use_for: Festive sale and launch announcements to past buyers
Back-in-stock, price-drop and cart reminders (marketing category)
Appointment and order updates (utility category)
Restaurant, salon and clinic re-engagement offers
Event and webinar reminders
avoid: Messaging people who never opted in: WhatsApp Business requires opt-in and blocks or reports hurt the number's quality
One-way updates to a public following: use genre:whatsapp_channel_post
Shareable text for groups: use genre:whatsapp_forward
Long newsletters in a chat bubble: send a short note with a link, or use email
Marketing copy filed as a utility template to dodge the category: Meta categorises templates (Marketing, Utility, Authentication) and charges by category
Plain SMS campaigns: use genre:sms_marketing (DLT rules differ)

sources.title: Meta for Developers: WhatsApp message template components
sources.supports: body max 1024 characters; header text max 60; footer max 60; button label max 25; up to 10 buttons, at most 2 URL buttons and 1 phone number button

sources.title: Meta for Developers: WhatsApp Business Platform pricing
sources.supports: effective July 1, 2025, Meta charges per message; templates are categorised as Marketing, Utility or Authentication; non-template messages are free (fetched 2026-10-05)

sources.title: WatEase: WhatsApp promotional messages (India)
sources.supports: Indian vendor library of promotional broadcast copy by occasion (low confidence, vendor content)

sources.title: Economic Times: D2C brands turn to WhatsApp to win new customers (2026-06-18)
sources.supports: GoKwik report: about 83% of WhatsApp-generated orders in the Oct-Dec festive quarter came from first-time buyers (evidence for status rising)

buyers: Agencies and WhatsApp business-solution vendors writing for clients
cards.value_why: Indian WhatsApp vendors publish occasion-wise message libraries for brands (low-confidence vendor content), and ET (2026-06-18) reports D2C brands using WhatsApp to acquire first-time buyers; the copy is short and often bundled into CRM retainers.
cards.goal: The customer taps the button (shop, book, reply) and does not block or report the number.

structure.does: Template name, category (Marketing, Utility or Authentication), language, and sample values for each variable for Meta's review.
Image, video or a short text header naming the offer or occasion.

Greeting with the customer's name variable, why this message now (their past purchase, the occasion, the item they saved), the specific offer (what, price or discount, until when), one line of value. Use *bold* for the one key fact.
structure.length: Up to 1024 characters; aim for 40-90 words

structure.does: Brand name and an opt-out line.
One URL button for the main action and a quick reply such as 'Stop offers'.

length.note: Body words. The hard limit is 1024 characters, but a chat bubble is read on a phone in a few seconds; utility reminders can be 25-40 words, festive offers with a story up to about 100.

checklist: Is the template category stated and does the copy fit it?
Does the body say why the customer is getting this message now?
Is the offer specific (item, price or discount, end date)?
Is the body within 1024 characters and the header and footer within 60?
Is there one main button with a label of 25 characters or fewer?
Is there an opt-out line or a 'Stop' quick reply?
Are variables marked ({{1}}, {{2}}) with sample values?
Is any deadline real and any 'free' truly free?
pitfalls: 'Dear Customer' with no reason for the message: it reads as spam and gets blocked. Use the name variable and the trigger ('the kurta you saved is back in your size').
Emoji walls and ALL CAPS: one or two emoji and *bold* for the key fact are enough.
Several offers in one template: one offer, one button.
Sending marketing templates daily: every message is now charged per delivery and every block hurts quality. Send fewer, better-timed messages.
Fake urgency ('Last 2 pieces!' when stock is fine): a listed dark pattern under the CCPA guidelines.
No way out: add a 'Stop offers' quick reply or opt-out line; people who cannot opt out block instead.
cards.exemplar_brief: WhatsApp marketing template for a Lucknow chikankari kurta brand's pre-Diwali sale (20% off, ending on a date given as [date]), sent to opted-in past buyers; Hinglish (Roman); template category and variable samples, header, body under 600 characters with {{1}} name and {{2}} code, footer with opt-out, one URL button 'Shop the sale' and a quick reply 'Stop offers'; goal: tap through to the sale page.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp1 V2 C1. Category Marketing with variable samples, text header (39 chars), body with {{1}} name and {{2}} code, *bold* on the key fact, end date, footer with opt-out (49 chars), one URL button 'Shop the sale' and a 'Stop offers' quick reply; language-filing choice flagged; natural Hinglish ('isliye sale ki khabar sabse pehle aapko'). Competent but thin: the value line ('Lucknow se seedha aapke ghar') says nothing about the chikankari itself, and 'sabse pehle aapko' is an early-access claim the brand must make true or drop.

cards.name: WhatsApp Channel post
cards.summary: A one-way update to a WhatsApp Channel's followers, read on a phone in a few seconds, often with a link, poll or media. Good looks like the news or value in the first bold line, one or two lines of context, and a call to action followers can actually take (react, vote, tap), since they cannot reply.
use_for: Publisher and local-news updates and alerts
Brand drops, launches and behind-the-scenes
Creator updates and new-video links
Civic, government and campus announcements
Polls for quick audience feedback
avoid: Personalised offers to customers: use genre:whatsapp_broadcast (the WhatsApp Business template product)
Text written to be forwarded in family and community groups: use genre:whatsapp_forward
Telegram channels with longer posts: use genre:telegram_channel_post
Asking followers to 'reply' or 'DM us': they cannot reply in a channel; use a poll, reactions or a link

sources.title: afaqs: Meta's WhatsApp Channels: the future of global brand messaging or Threads 2.0?
sources.supports: Indian trade-press coverage of WhatsApp Channels as a one-way broadcast surface for brands, publishers and creators

sources.title: Meta for Developers: WhatsApp text messages
sources.supports: WhatsApp hyperlinks URLs in body text automatically (used for formatting guidance; no official Channel post limit was found on 2026-10-04)

buyers: News publishers and local media startups
Government departments, political offices and institutions
cards.value_why: Indian trade press (afaqs) covers WhatsApp Channels as a brand and publisher broadcast surface; demand is India-heavy and usually bundled into social-media retainers rather than bought per post.
cards.goal: The follower reads the update on one screen and reacts, votes or taps the link.

structure.does: The news or value in about ten words, in *bold*. Front-load the place, number or name that matters.
What it means for the follower or what to do; short lines with breaks.
Image, video, voice note or poll that carries the post; the text works as its caption.
One thing to do: tap a link, vote in the poll, react with a named emoji.
Source for news claims, or the brand's short sign-off.

length.note: No official character limit for Channel posts was found (harvest, 2026-10-04); length is set by the phone screen. Alerts can be 15-30 words; a story teaser with context up to about 90.

checklist: Does the first line carry the news or value on its own?
Is the post readable on one phone screen without 'Read more'?
Is there exactly one action followers can take without replying?
Does it avoid asking followers to reply, comment or DM?
Are news claims sourced and free of unverified rumours?
Is formatting limited to WhatsApp's own (*bold*, _italic_, line breaks)?
Is any AI-generated image or video that looks real labelled?
pitfalls: 'Reply YES to get the link': followers cannot reply in a channel. Put the link in the post or use a poll.
Copy-pasting the Instagram caption with ten hashtags: hashtags do nothing here; write for the chat screen.
Burying the news under a greeting ('Namaskar dosto, aaj hum baat karenge...'): lead with the fact.
Posting many times a day: followers mute the channel. Post when there is something worth the notification.
Unverified alerts during a crisis ('Schools shut tomorrow, forward karo'): one wrong alert costs the channel's trust; confirm with the official source and name it.
Realistic AI images of real events without a label: the 2026 IT Rules amendment requires prominent labels on synthetic audio-visual content.

ban.label: asks for replies followers cannot send

cards.exemplar_brief: Three WhatsApp Channel posts for a Jaipur city-news startup during a monsoon week: a waterlogging traffic alert with diversions (roads as [placeholders]), a poll asking which ward needs drain cleaning first, and a link post to the day's explainer; Hinglish (Roman); each 20-60 words with a bold lead line and one action; no reply requests; goal: react, vote or tap the link.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V1 C1. Three posts, 28-40 words each, bold lead lines, one action each (live-update link, vote, explainer link), no reply/comment asks, no hashtags, one emoji; the alert names its source and time, the poll promises a result 'kal subah isi channel par', the explainer link gives reading time. Writer fault: the poll question 'Aapke ward mein naali ki safai sabse pehle kahan honi chahiye?' asks where inside the reader's ward while the options are four wards; it should ask 'Kis ward mein ... sabse pehle honi chahiye?' Placeholders for roads, wards and the explainer finding are as briefed.

cards.name: WhatsApp good-morning / broadcast forward
cards.summary: Short, shareable text written to travel through Indian WhatsApp groups: a good-morning suvichar, an original thought, a festival line or a community notice. Good looks like one idea that fits one phone screen, plain Hindi or Hinglish the sender's mother would forward, a sender line at the end so the source travels with it, and nothing fabricated: no fake quotes, no unverified news.
use_for: Good-morning suvichar for community, religious and senior-citizen groups
Broadcast lists of political workers, NGOs and associations
RWA, school-parent and samaj notices meant to be passed on
Festival and observance lines from local businesses
Awareness messages (health camps, scams, civic drives)
avoid: A brand offer to customers: use genre:whatsapp_broadcast
Updates to a public following on a Channel: use genre:whatsapp_channel_post
A festival campaign creative for a brand: use genre:festival_greeting
Quotes attributed to famous people that they never said: write an original line or quote with a checked source
'Forward to 10 people or face bad luck' chain pressure and unverified 'breaking' news: they spread misinformation and damage the sender's name

sources.title: MeitY: IT Rules amendment on synthetically generated information (G.S.R. 120(E), 2026)
sources.supports: realistic synthetic audio-visual content must be prominently labelled; synthetic content falsely depicting real people or events is a class platforms must act on

buyers: Political parties' and leaders' social media and IT teams
NGOs and health or awareness campaigns
Local businesses greeting their customer lists
cards.value_why: Enormous unpaid consumer volume; paid only when political, religious or community organisations run broadcast lists (harvest note, 2026-10-04).
cards.goal: The reader feels something or learns one useful thing in five seconds and forwards it with the sender line intact.

structure.does: Greeting or label that signals the type: 'सुप्रभात', 'Aaj ka vichar', 'Zaroori soochna'. One emoji at most.
One thought (suvichar), one wish or one notice. For notices: what, when, where, who to contact.
A line that turns the thought into something to do today.
'- [Organisation or name], [place]' so the forward carries its source. A hyphen reads as cleanly as a dash.

length.note: One phone screen. Suvichar and wishes are 10-40 words; community notices with dates and contacts up to about 80. The lint caps (max_words 120, max_emoji 4, sender line) apply per message: check each message from its own file, never several messages in one file.

checklist: Does the message carry one idea only?
Does it fit one phone screen without 'Read more'?
Is every quote either original or attributed to a source that was checked?
Is every factual claim (date, scheme, health tip) verified?
Is there no chain pressure ('forward to 10 people', 'bad luck if you don't')?
Does it end with a sender line?
Are emoji limited to one or two?
In election periods, does political content follow the Model Code and carry no unlabelled synthetic media?
pitfalls: Fake attribution ('— A.P.J. Abdul Kalam' under a line he never said): it erodes trust in the sender the moment someone checks. Write an original line and sign it with the sender's name.
Health 'tips' that are folk claims ('haldi cures cancer'): misleading and dangerous; share only what a health authority says, and name it.
Long paragraphs: forwards are read in a scroll of fifty messages. Short lines, one idea.
Political forwards with doctored images or invented statistics: synthetic media rules and defamation law both bite; stick to verifiable facts and label any AI visual.
Missing sender line: the message travels anonymously and the organisation gets no credit. End with '- Name, place'.
Over-decorated text (rows of 🌹🙏🌸): one emoji is warmer than ten.

require.label: ends with a sender line (- Name)

cards.exemplar_brief: Seven good-morning suvichar forwards, one per day of the week (Monday to Sunday), for a Varanasi senior-citizens' yoga group's WhatsApp broadcast list; Hindi in Devanagari; each 15-40 words with one original thought on health, patience or family (no quotes attributed to famous people), at most two emoji, and the sender line '- गंगा तट योग समूह, वाराणसी'; goal: members read them and forward with the sender line intact. Write each message to its own file and check each from its own file: the word and emoji caps apply per message.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C2. Seven original suvichar (Mon-Sun), 29-35 words each, one 🙏 each, each one idea on health, patience or family, all ending with the exact sender line. Varanasi-specific images without cliche (ghat steps climbed one at a time, Ganga that is never in a hurry yet reaches the sea), practical and age-aware ('आपके घुटनों की अपनी चाल है'), and lines worth forwarding ('परिवार को आपकी सलाह से पहले आपका साथ चाहिए'). No attributed quotes, no medical claims, no chain pressure. Clean Devanagari. The writer's lint_suspect is correct: each message passes alone; only the combined file trips the per-message caps. CARD FIX: lint -> mark max_words 120 / max_emoji 4 as per message (or make exemplar_brief say 'check each message from its own file'), since the exemplar asks for seven messages in one file; exemplar_brief 'one per weekday' -> 'one per day of the week (Monday to Sunday)', since seven is not the number of weekdays. | CARD FIXED 2026-10-07 (fix_genre_d): exemplar_brief: 'one per weekday' -> 'one per day of the week (Monday to Sunday)' plus check-each-message-from-its-own-file instruction; length note says lint caps are per message; re-judge pending.

cards.name: White paper
cards.summary: An authoritative, research-backed document that explains a costly problem and argues for an approach, written to educate B2B buyers and their evaluators. Good looks like an executive summary a CFO can act on, a problem section built on cited data, a fair comparison of current approaches, a vendor-neutral framework, and the product kept to the last page.
use_for: B2B technology, fintech and cybersecurity buyers who need a business case
Technical white papers explaining an architecture or method to evaluators
Gated lead magnets for considered, high-value purchases
Sales enablement: a document a champion forwards inside their company
Industry-association and consultancy position papers
avoid: A product brochure with a white-paper cover: buyers spot it and stop reading; use genre:brochure_copy or genre:one_pager
Original survey data as the main story: use genre:research_report
Recommendations to government: use genre:policy_brief
A lighter, visual, top-of-funnel download: use genre:ebook_lead_magnet
Statistics without sources: every number needs a citation the reader can check

sources.title: Upwork: 14 Types of Freelance Writing Jobs and What They Pay (published 2026-01-21)
sources.supports: white papers listed among technical-writer and business-writer projects; business writers typically $25-$50/hr on Upwork

sources.title: Upwork: Best Freelance White Paper Writers for Hire
sources.supports: dedicated hire page for white paper writers

sources.title: EFA 2026 Rate Chart (2026-03-18)
sources.supports: Ghostwriting > Business/marketing: 50.0¢-$1.00 per word, $87.50-$125.00 per hour

buyers: B2B SaaS, fintech and cybersecurity companies
Product marketing and sales enablement teams
cards.value_why: Upwork runs a dedicated white-paper writer hire page and lists business writers at $25-$50/hr (2026-01-21); the EFA 2026 rate chart puts business/marketing ghostwriting at 50¢-$1.00 per word and $87.50-$125/hr, among the higher writing rates.
cards.goal: A B2B buyer or evaluator finishes convinced the problem is costly and the approach is right, shares it internally, and asks for a conversation or demo.

structure.does: Names the problem and the promise plainly; no product name.
The problem, what it costs, the recommended approach and the next step, readable on its own by a senior reader.
Market context and the cost of the problem with cited data, a concrete scenario from the reader's world (Indian regulation, rupee figures where relevant).
2-4 common approaches compared fairly: where each works and where it breaks.
A vendor-neutral framework: principles, how it works, what it needs, with a diagram described in words.
A case example or pilot result the client can document and has permission to share.
Questions to ask vendors or steps to implement; a page a champion can forward on its own.
One next step, then a short company description at the very end.
Numbered citations with titles, publishers, dates and links.

length.note: Driven by the complexity of the problem and how technical the evaluator is. A business-case paper for executives sits near the low end; a technical white paper for architects runs longer. Past about 7,000 words, split it.

checklist: Can the executive summary be read alone and still give the recommendation?
Is every statistic cited with source and date, or marked [source needed]?
Are current approaches compared fairly, including where they work?
Is the framework vendor-neutral, with the product kept to the end?
Is there at least one documented case or example?
Are subheads descriptive enough to skim the argument from them alone?
Is there an evaluation checklist or roadmap the reader can use?
Is there one clear next step?
Is there a numbered reference list?
pitfalls: Product pitch from page two: the evaluator closes it. Keep the company to the conclusion and 'about' block; let the approach sell it.
Statistics from memory or from a blog that cites nothing: trace each number to its original report or remove it; one wrong figure discredits the paper.
Strawman comparisons ('legacy tools are slow and outdated'): name what the alternatives do well; fairness is what makes the recommendation believable.
An executive summary that is an introduction ('This paper explores...'): state the conclusion and the cost in the first paragraph.
Hype words ('revolutionary', 'best-in-class'): replace each with a measurable claim the client can back.
Gated with a form that collects more data than needed: ask for what you will use and state the purpose (DPDP regime).
cards.exemplar_brief: Executive summary plus the problem and 'why current approaches fall short' sections (1,500-2,000 words) of a white paper by a Bengaluru fintech-infrastructure startup: 'Reconciling UPI collections at scale for mid-size Indian NBFCs'; audience: NBFC CFOs and heads of operations; formal Indian English; vendor-neutral; every statistic cited or marked [source needed]; goal: download-to-demo request.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. Title and subtitle name the problem and promise with no product; executive summary stands alone (problem, costs, the one argument, what the paper delivers); problem section walks a concrete Rs 4,250 payment-link EMI through aggregator, settlement file, bank line and LMS to a wrong collections call, then the four records, five failure patterns and four costs; every figure is [source needed] and every RBI/NPCI point (settlement timing, dispute TAT, Fair Practices Code, bureau reporting frequency, SBR Middle Layer) is [verify] rather than asserted; four current approaches each credited with where they work before where they break, then three shared limits; formal Indian English ('lakhs of payments'); numbered references. Nit: the executive summary ends on 'the full paper ends with a checklist' rather than the demo next step the goal needs.
